questions.subject: GEOMETRY
questions.learningObjective: describe the constant ratio between corresponding sides of similar figures
questions.stem: Two photographs are taken of the same bridge, one from far away and one from close by, and in each the piers, the roadway, and the cables are all in the same proportions. What single fact about the two photographs defines them as similar figures?

options.text: One can be turned into the other by one single scale factor
One can be turned into the other by one single translation alone
options.misconception: confuses a change of size with a change of position

options.text: Both photographs enclose exactly the same area on the paper
options.misconception: believes matching areas is what makes two figures similar

options.text: Both photographs show every pier at exactly the same height
options.misconception: demands one absolute length to match instead of a constant ratio

questions.explanation: Similar figures have all their corresponding sides in one and the same ratio, all their corresponding angles equal, and no others, which is the same as saying one figure is a single uniform enlargement or reduction of the other. That uniform change of size is the scale factor, and applying it to every side at once is what makes the shapes correspond. A translation moves a figure without resizing it, equal areas on the paper say nothing about proportion, and one shared absolute length could be produced by figures of quite different shapes.
questions.hint: Ask whether one figure could be produced from the other by resizing alone.

questions.subject: GEOMETRY
questions.learningObjective: state the two-angle criterion that forces two triangles to be similar
questions.stem: A surveyor has two triangles with no side lengths measured at all, and claims they are similar. Which pair of angle facts would be enough on its own to justify the claim?

options.text: Two angles of one triangle equal two angles of the other triangle
One angle of one triangle equal to one angle of the other triangle
options.misconception: believes a single matching angle settles the shape of both triangles

options.text: Two sides of one triangle equal to two sides of the other triangle
options.misconception: relies on side lengths alone, which fix no angles at all

options.text: The perimeters of the two triangles standing in one constant ratio
options.misconception: uses one summary length, which hides the shape of the figure

questions.explanation: Two matching angles are enough because the third is then forced, since the interior angles of a triangle total 180 degrees, so matching two leaves the third matching too, and a triangle is pinned down by its angles up to a single uniform scaling. That is why two angles are the criterion and one is not: with only one angle fixed, a triangle can still be stretched sideways while keeping that angle, so its shape is not determined. Side lengths and perimeters describe size rather than shape, which is the opposite of what the criterion needs.
questions.hint: Ask how many angles a triangle has, and what that implies about fixing its shape.

questions.subject: GEOMETRY
questions.learningObjective: describe what a scale factor above one does to lengths and to area
questions.stem: A map is redrawn so that every length on it is four times what it was, while the shapes it shows are all left exactly as they are in proportion. Compared with the first map, what has happened to the area enclosed by each shape?

options.text: It has grown by a factor of sixteen, the square of the length factor
It has grown by a factor of four, the same as the length factor
options.misconception: reuses the linear factor for the area and so understates the growth

options.text: It has grown by a factor of eight, halfway between four and sixteen
options.misconception: invents a mean value between the linear and area factors

options.text: It has grown by a factor of twelve, which is four added to eight
options.misconception: adds figures rather than multiplying them, which has no basis

questions.explanation: Every length in a figure is multiplied by the scale factor, and an area is built from two lengths in each direction, so the enlargement acts twice and the area grows by the square of the scale factor. With a factor of four that square is sixteen, so the area is sixteen times what it was. Applying the linear factor of four to the area is the classic slip, and it understates the growth by a factor of the scale factor itself, which grows without bound as the enlargement gets larger.
questions.hint: Count how many lengths go into building one square unit of area.

questions.subject: GEOMETRY
questions.learningObjective: relate the area ratio of similar figures to their linear ratio
questions.stem: Two similar windows are glazed, and the first is 3 units wide where the second is 2 units wide, the proportions matching throughout. In what ratio do the two areas of glass stand to each other?

options.text: 9 to 4, because each linear ratio has to be squared
3 to 2, because that is the ratio of the two widths
options.misconception: reuses the linear ratio and forgets that area builds from two lengths

options.text: 6 to 5, because the two linear ratios are simply added together
options.misconception: adds the two side lengths instead of multiplying each by itself

options.text: 5 to 3, because the areas lie between the two linear ratios
options.misconception: takes a figure between the linear and squared values

Squaring is what turns 3 into 9 and 2 into 4, and it is unavoidable because a region grows in both directions at once, not in one. The linear ratio of 3 to 2 is a perfectly good answer to a question about widths, but not to one about areas.
questions.hint: The two directions of the region are each stretched, so square both parts of the ratio.

questions.learningObjective: apply the dilation rule when the centre of scaling is the origin
questions.stem: A star sticker sits on a sheet of tracing paper with one of its tips at the point (4, -2), and the paper is then fed through a machine that enlarges every mark on it from the corner where the axes cross. What happens to that tip?

options.text: Each coordinate is multiplied by the same scale factor, so the tip moves out along its ray
Each coordinate keeps its value, since the origin itself never moves
options.misconception: believes a fixed centre freezes every point of the figure

options.text: The two coordinates are added together to give one new coordinate value
options.misconception: adds the coordinates instead of scaling each of them

options.text: The two coordinates are multiplied against each other to give one value
options.misconception: multiplies the two coordinates together rather than by the factor

questions.explanation: A dilation centred at the origin measures each point from the origin, scales that distance, and lays it down again along the same ray, and on a coordinate grid that works out to multiplying each coordinate by the scale factor in turn. So a factor of three would take (4, -2) to (12, -6), with the point staying on the same ray from the origin while moving further out. The origin staying put is a statement about that one point, not about the rest of the figure, and combining the two coordinates loses the direction of the ray entirely.
questions.hint: Each point is measured from the centre, scaled, and replaced along the same ray.

questions.topic: Dilation about a point away from the origin
questions.learningObjective: apply the dilation rule when the centre of scaling is not the origin
questions.stem: A model kite is scaled up about a peg at the point (2, 5) rather than about the corner where the axes cross. What is true of the peg itself and of the other marked points on the kite?

The peg moves as well, since the whole figure is being enlarged

options.text: The peg stays put, and every other point moves parallel to the first one
options.misconception: sends the points sideways instead of away from the peg

options.text: The peg stays put, and every other point keeps its distance from the peg
options.misconception: treats a dilation as though it left the figure's size alone

The only way to get this right away from the origin is to remember that the distances being scaled are measured from the peg and not from the corner of the grid.
questions.hint: Measure every distance from the centre of scaling, and remember its distance from itself.

questions.subject: GEOMETRY
questions.learningObjective: describe a translation as a single displacement vector
questions.stem: A robot on a warehouse floor starts at the point (2, 3) and later stands at the point (7, -1), having slid the whole way without turning. How is that slide best described?

options.text: As one displacement vector applied to every point, with nothing resized
As a single stretch about the starting point that made the robot larger
options.misconception: mixes a change of position in with a change of size

options.text: As a half turn about the middle of the two points, which returned the robot
options.misconception: describes a turn that would undo the move rather than make it

options.text: As two separate moves, one along each axis, each with its own vector
options.misconception: splits one displacement into two and loses its single direction

questions.explanation: A translation is a rigid move: every point of the figure shifts by the same displacement and nothing about the figure itself changes size or shape. The displacement is recorded as one vector with a horizontal part and a vertical part, and here it is 5 to the right and 4 down, so the whole slide is described by that single pair of numbers. Nothing is stretched, turned, or reflected, and splitting the move in two loses the fact that it is one translation with one direction rather than two separate ones.
questions.hint: Ask whether anything about the figure's size or shape changed during the slide.

questions.subject: GEOMETRY
questions.learningObjective: describe what a rotation by a stated angle about a point does
questions.stem: A turntable carries a marker at a point that is 6 units from the hub, and the turntable swings the marker through a quarter turn about that hub, going counterclockwise. What happens to the marker during that swing?

options.text: It stays 6 units from the hub and lands on a new ray a quarter turn round
It stays 6 units from the hub and lands back where it began
options.misconception: believes a quarter turn returns the marker to its start

options.text: It drifts to 3 units from the hub while the turntable carries it round
options.misconception: halves the radius during the turn, as though the swing shrank it

options.text: It holds its place and the hub swings around it instead
options.misconception: reverses which point is fixed and which one travels

Nothing about a rotation changes a distance from the centre, so the marker cannot drift inward, and the centre is the fixed point by definition rather than the travelling one.

questions.learningObjective: describe what reflection in a line does to a point
questions.stem: A pane of glass stands on a grid along the line x = 3, and a point marked at (1, 5) is seen in it. Where does the reflected image of that point fall?

options.text: At (5, 5), the same height and as far to the other side of the glass
At (2, 5), one unit off the glass on the original side
options.misconception: moves the point to the mirror line instead of across it

options.text: At (1, 6), the same horizontal position and one unit higher
options.misconception: reflects over a horizontal mirror line when the glass is vertical

options.text: At (3, 5), directly on the glass at the point's own height
options.misconception: lands the image on the mirror line rather than beside it

From (1, 5) to the line x = 3 the horizontal gap is 2, so the image sits 2 units past the glass, which is (5, 5). Because the glass is vertical it is the horizontal coordinate that changes, and a reflection never lands its image on the mirror line unless the point began there.

questions.subject: GEOMETRY
questions.learningObjective: describe the effect of applying two transformations in a stated order
questions.stem: A stamp is pressed onto a sheet of paper, and then the whole sheet is turned over and slid across the table. What can be said about the result of the two moves?

options.text: The two moves compose into a single rigid motion of the whole plane
The two moves cannot be combined, since a flip cannot be followed by a slide
options.misconception: believes two rigid moves can never be carried out one after the other

options.text: The two moves resize the pattern, since turning a sheet over changes its scale
options.misconception: supposes a flip is an enlargement rather than a rigid move

options.text: The two moves leave the pattern where it was, since they undo each other
options.misconception: assumes any two consecutive rigid moves cancel out

questions.explanation: A composition of transformations is simply the single map that results from applying them one after another, and any sequence of rigid motions composes into another rigid motion of the plane, so the pattern keeps its size and shape however many moves are chained. A reflection followed by a translation is the standard case, called a glide reflection, and it does not need the two steps to cancel. Two rigid moves never rescale anything, and they only undo each other in the special case where the second is the exact reverse of the first.
questions.hint: Ask whether the two moves together change the size or shape of the pattern.

questions.subject: GEOMETRY
questions.topic: Rigid motions and what they preserve
questions.learningObjective: state the measurements a rigid motion preserves
questions.stem: A sheet of paper is folded, turned over, slid, and turned again, and a pattern drawn on it is measured before and after. Which set of measurements must be identical in both states?

options.text: All lengths, all angles, and which sides are parallel to which
All lengths and all angles, but the parallel relations may be lost
options.misconception: thinks a rigid move can break parallel lines that were parallel

options.text: Only the lengths, since turning the paper over alters the angles it makes
options.misconception: believes a flip changes the angle a side makes with the horizontal

options.text: Only the angles, since sliding the paper alters the lengths between marks
options.misconception: believes a rigid move can stretch one distance while keeping angles

questions.explanation: A rigid motion is defined as one that changes where a figure sits without changing what it is, so every length, every angle, and every relationship of parallelism survives untouched. Translations, rotations, reflections, and any composition of them all have this property, which is why a folded and turned sheet still folds along the same lines. The one thing a reflection does change is which way a figure faces, so orientation is not on the list of things preserved, but measurements are.
questions.hint: Rigid means rigid: nothing about the measurements may move.

questions.subject: GEOMETRY
questions.learningObjective: describe a construction that finds the midpoint of a segment
questions.stem: A forester must mark the exact middle of a fallen tree trunk using only a compass and a straightedge, and no measuring tape is available. Which construction finds that middle point?

options.text: Arc from each end at one fixed width, then join the two crossings
Draw a circle about one end passing through the other end of the trunk
options.misconception: uses a circle about one end, which fixes no middle point at all

options.text: Measure along the top of the trunk and halve that distance by eye
options.misconception: relies on judging a distance rather than on a construction

options.text: Draw a line from one end of the trunk to the centre of its widest point
options.misconception: joins an end to a point that is not the midpoint of the segment

questions.explanation: The construction uses the fact that two points standing equally far from both ends of a segment lie on its perpendicular bisector, and that is exactly what equal-width arcs produce. A circle about one end merely reproduces the trunk's own length and tells you nothing about where the middle lies.
questions.hint: Look for the two points that are each equally far from both ends.

questions.learningObjective: state the equidistance property of a perpendicular bisector
questions.stem: Two park gates are to be joined by a fence, and a sign is to stand at a spot from which the two gates are exactly the same distance away. Along which line may that sign be placed?

Along the straight line joining the two gates themselves
options.misconception: puts the sign on the line, where the two distances cannot match

options.text: Along the circle whose radius is half the distance between the two gates
options.misconception: answers with a closed curve instead of the required straight line

options.text: Along any line through the point where the two gates meet
options.misconception: invents a meeting point, though the two gates are separate posts

Two separate gates have no common point to pivot about, which rules out the last suggestion.

At (6, 8), which is the position of the second marker itself

questions.learningObjective: find the slope of a line perpendicular to a line of known slope
questions.stem: A ramp climbs with a rise of 3 units for every 4 units along the ground, and a second ramp is laid across the first at a right angle. What is the rise-over-run slope of that second ramp?

options.text: Negative four thirds, the negative reciprocal of three fourths
Negative three fourths, the first ramp's slope with a minus sign
options.misconception: negates the slope instead of inverting it as well

options.text: Four thirds, the reciprocal of the first ramp's slope with no sign
options.misconception: inverts the slope but forgets the sign the right angle forces

options.text: Negative three fourths, which is the first ramp's slope read backwards
options.misconception: reverses rise and run, which gives a different figure entirely

Simply negating the original slope, or inverting it while keeping the sign, each gives a line that meets the first at some angle but not a right one.

questions.learningObjective: read the angle of inclination of a line from its slope

questions.learningObjective: recognise a quadrilateral with two distinct pairs of adjacent equal sides

questions.stem: Two similar fields have areas of 64 hectares and 144 hectares, and a student divides one area by the other and reports 9 to 4 as the ratio of the fields' corresponding side lengths. What is wrong with that step?

options.text: A side length follows the square root of the area ratio, so it is 8 to 12
A side length follows the area ratio directly, so dividing was correct
options.misconception: believes areas and lengths scale by one and the same factor

options.text: A side length follows the cube root of the area ratio, so it is 4 to 5
options.misconception: borrows the exponent that belongs to volumes rather than to areas

options.text: A side length cannot be recovered from areas without the shapes being given
options.misconception: claims the shape is missing when the ratio already fixes it

questions.explanation: An area ratio is the square of the corresponding linear ratio, so the linear ratio is recovered by taking the square root of the area ratio in each direction. The square root of 64 is 8 and the square root of 144 is 12, so the side lengths stand in the ratio 8 to 12, which reduces to 2 to 3, and indeed 8 times 8 is 64 while 12 times 12 is 144. Dividing areas directly treats a two-dimensional measurement as though it were a one-dimensional one, and the square root is exactly the operation that undoes the squaring.
questions.hint: The area ratio is the square of the linear ratio, so undo the squaring.

questions.subject: GEOMETRY
questions.topic: Dilation measured from the wrong centre
questions.learningObjective: correct a dilation computed from the origin instead of its stated centre
questions.stem: A drawing on a grid is enlarged by a scale factor of 3 about the point (2, 1). A student multiplies the coordinates of the point (4, 3) by 3 and reports the image as (12, 9). What is the mistake?

options.text: The scaled distances must be measured from (2, 1), giving the point (8, 7)
The scale factor of 3 was applied twice over, once to each coordinate
options.misconception: blames a doubled factor rather than the wrong centre of scaling

options.text: The point (2, 1) is the centre and so cannot have an image at all
options.misconception: denies the centre an image instead of naming the wrong centre

options.text: Dilation coordinates are only ever added to the centre, never multiplied
options.misconception: believes a dilation can only ever translate the figure

questions.explanation: The offsets from the stated centre are 4 minus 2, which is 2, and 3 minus 1, which is 2, and tripling them gives 6 in each direction. Adding those back to the centre gives 2 plus 6 and 1 plus 6, which is the point (8, 7), so that is the image. Multiplying the raw coordinates scales the drawing about the corner where the axes cross instead, which is a different enlargement altogether, and the corner and the pin are 2 units apart in each direction here, so the two answers are genuinely different points.
questions.hint: Check which point the distances are being measured from.

questions.subject: GEOMETRY
questions.topic: Coordinate swap used for the wrong mirror
questions.learningObjective: correct a coordinate swap used in place of a slanted reflection
questions.stem: A student is told to reflect the point (3, 1) in the slanted line y = 2x and simply exchanges the two coordinates, reporting the image as (1, 3). What is wrong with the reasoning?

options.text: Exchanging coordinates reflects in y = x, and a slanted mirror needs its foot
Exchanging coordinates reflects in the line x = y, which is the same line
options.misconception: claims two different slanted lines are really one line

options.text: Exchanging coordinates reflects in the horizontal axis, not in a slanted line
options.misconception: misnames which axis the exchange reflects the point in

options.text: Exchanging coordinates is correct and the slope of the mirror does not matter
options.misconception: believes the slope of the mirror cannot affect a reflection

questions.explanation: Exchanging the two coordinates reflects a point in the line y = x and in no other line, so the shortcut simply does not apply to the line y = 2x, which has a different slope altogether. A general reflection needs the foot of the perpendicular on the mirror, and for (3, 1) on y = 2x that foot is at (1, 2), so the true image is twice the foot minus the point, which is (-1, 3) rather than (1, 3). The slope of the mirror decides which shortcut is available, so it cannot be dismissed as irrelevant.
questions.hint: The coordinate swap works for exactly one mirror line. Which one?

questions.subject: GEOMETRY
questions.topic: Why areas scale as the square
questions.learningObjective: explain why the area ratio of similar figures is the square of the linear ratio
questions.stem: Explain why the areas of two similar figures stand in the square of the ratio of their corresponding sides, and identify the step that makes the squaring unavoidable.

answer.exemplar: A dilation with scale factor k takes every point of a figure to a new point measured from the same centre along the same ray, at k times the distance. So a region that is measured a units across in one direction and b units across in the other becomes a region measured k a across and k b across. Its area is a product of two lengths, namely a times b, and after the dilation that product is k a times k b, which is k squared times a times b. The squaring is unavoidable because the area is built from two lengths rather than one, and the dilation acts on each of them independently, so the factor has to appear once for each direction. This also explains why the linear factor is the wrong answer for an area: it accounts for only one of the two stretches, and it understates the true growth by a factor of k, which becomes more and more serious as the enlargement grows.

questions.subject: GEOMETRY
questions.topic: Why a perpendicular bisector gives equal distances
questions.learningObjective: explain why every point on a perpendicular bisector is equidistant from the endpoints
questions.stem: Explain why every point on the perpendicular bisector of a segment is exactly as far from one endpoint as from the other, and say why the converse also holds.

answer.exemplar: Let the segment have endpoints A and B, let M be its midpoint, and let P be any point on the line through M at a right angle to the segment. Consider the two triangles formed by P, M, and each endpoint in turn. In the first, the side PM is shared with the second, the side MA equals MB because M is the midpoint, and the angle at M is a right angle in both triangles because the line is perpendicular to the segment. Two triangles with a shared side, a second matching side, and the included angle equal are congruent, so the third sides match, which says that the distance from P to A equals the distance from P to B. So every point on the line is equidistant, and the two congruent triangles in fact lie as mirror images across the line PM. The converse holds for the same reason in the other direction: if a point is equidistant from A and B it lies on the perpendicular bisector, since the locus of such points is exactly that line, which is why the compass-and-straightedge construction of crossing arcs produces it in the first place.

questions.subject: GEOMETRY
questions.learningObjective: explain why a rigid motion leaves lengths and angles unchanged
questions.stem: Explain why a translation, a rotation, a reflection, or any sequence of them leaves every length and every angle of a figure untouched, and say what it does change.

answer.exemplar: Each of the three moves is built out of pieces that leave distances alone. A translation adds the same displacement to every point, so the difference between any two points is unchanged, and every length and every angle is a statement about differences between points, so all of them survive. A rotation fixes a centre and turns every point about it by the same angle, so each point keeps its distance from the centre, and since every pair distance is fixed by the two centre distances and the angle between them, the whole figure keeps all of its measurements. A reflection is a flip in a line, which is a mirror image and so preserves every measurement while reversing the sense of the angles. The thing that does change is not a measurement but an orientation: a reflection, and only a reflection among the three, turns a clockwise ordering into a counterclockwise one, which is why congruence distinguishes the two kinds. Chaining the moves together changes nothing about this, because each step preserves everything and so their composition does as well.

questions.subject: GEOMETRY
questions.learningObjective: explain why two matching angles are enough to force two triangles to be similar
questions.stem: Explain why two pairs of matching angles are enough to prove that two triangles are similar, and say why a single matching pair is not.

answer.exemplar: The angles of a triangle total 180 degrees, so if two angles of one triangle equal two angles of another, the third angles must be equal as well, since each is found by subtracting the two known angles from the same fixed total of 180 degrees. The two triangles therefore have all three angles matching, and matching angles with one overall size is exactly what similarity means, since a triangle is determined in shape by its angles and can then be grown or shrunk by one uniform factor to match the other exactly. One matching pair is not enough, because a triangle can be stretched sideways while keeping a single angle fixed: hold one side and its opposite angle and the other two sides can still be changed, giving a long thin triangle and a short fat one with the same angle between them. That freedom is why the criterion needs two pairs, and it is the same freedom that makes two sides and one non-right angle an insufficient test.

questions.subject: GEOMETRY
questions.topic: Bisecting a segment, step by step
questions.learningObjective: order the steps of a segment bisection construction
questions.stem: Four labelled statements describe a compass-and-straightedge construction that finds the exact middle of a straight segment. Put them in the order in which they must occur, earliest first.

options.text: Open the compass wider than half the segment and strike arcs from each end
Draw the straight line that joins the two pairs of arc crossings
Mark the point where that new line meets the original segment
Set the compass to half the segment and mark one crossing only
options.misconception: believes a single crossing at half the width is enough to fix the midpoint

questions.explanation: The arcs have to come first, because they create the points that everything later depends on, and the compass must be opened wider than half the segment so that the arcs from opposite ends actually cross above and below it. The straight line through those crossings comes next, and it is the perpendicular bisector since each crossing is equally far from both ends. Only then can the point where that line meets the original segment be marked as the midpoint, so the order is forced, while a single crossing struck at half the width would not be equally far from the two ends and so proves nothing.
questions.hint: Nothing can be joined together until the points to join have been created.

questions.subject: GEOMETRY
questions.topic: Finding a circle's centre, step by step
questions.learningObjective: order the steps for locating a circle's centre from a marked diameter
questions.stem: Four labelled statements describe how to find the centre of a circle on a grid when the two ends of one of its diameters are already marked. Put them in the order in which they must occur, earliest first.

options.text: Average the two coordinates of each marked end to locate the point between them
Measure the straight distance from that point to either marked end
Report half of that distance as the circle's radius
Read the whole diameter's length off the grid and report that as the radius
options.misconception: confuses the full width of the circle with the half width

questions.explanation: The midpoint has to be found first, because it is the centre and every other quantity is measured from it, and the midpoint comes from averaging the two coordinates in each direction. The distance from that centre to a marked end is then the radius outright, so the final halving applies only when the working has measured the full diameter instead, which is a different route to the same figure. Treating the diameter as the radius would place the boundary twice as far out as the marked points, which is impossible since they already lie on it.
questions.hint: The centre comes from the two marked ends, and everything else is measured from it.

questions.subject: GEOMETRY
questions.topic: Dilation about a named centre, step by step
questions.learningObjective: order the steps for applying a dilation whose centre is not the origin
questions.stem: Four labelled statements describe how to find the image of a point P when a figure is dilated about a centre C that is not the origin. Put them in the order in which they must occur, earliest first.

options.text: Measure the offset of the point from the named centre of the dilation
Multiply that offset by the scale factor to get the new distance from the centre
Add the scaled offset back onto the centre to place the image point
Multiply the raw coordinates of the point by the scale factor and stop there
options.misconception: stops at the origin case and never returns to the named centre

questions.explanation: The offset from the named centre has to be taken first, because that is the quantity a dilation scales, and taking it from the origin instead silently enlarges the figure about the wrong point. The scale factor then turns that offset into the new distance from the centre, and the last step adds it back onto the centre to place the image on the correct ray. Skipping the final addition leaves a bare offset rather than a point, and it is exactly the step that reduces to coordinate multiplication when the centre happens to be the origin.
questions.hint: The offset must be taken and returned to the same centre.

questions.subject: GEOMETRY
questions.learningObjective: order the tests that identify a quadrilateral as a square
questions.stem: Four labelled statements describe a sequence of tests that settles whether an unnamed quadrilateral is a square. Put them in the order in which they must occur, earliest first.

options.text: Check that both pairs of opposite sides are parallel to establish a parallelogram
Check that the four sides are all equal in length
Conclude the figure is a square only once both the equal sides and right angles hold
Conclude the figure is a square as soon as the two diagonals measure the same
options.misconception: treats matching diagonals as sufficient, ignoring the sides and angles

questions.explanation: The parallel test has to come first, because a square is a parallelogram before it is anything more specific, and every later name in the family presupposes it. The equal-side check comes next and settles the rhombus condition, while a right angle, also present, settles the rectangle condition, and it is only once both of those hold on a parallelogram that the figure can be called a square. Equal diagonals alone settle nothing at all here, since an isosceles trapezoid has equal diagonals without being a square, so the diagonals cannot carry the conclusion.
questions.hint: The most specific name can only be used once the general ones are settled.
